newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Oil-rich Nigeria faces shutdown over fuel crisis.
newsitem.headline: Oil-rich Nigeria faces shutdown over fuel crisis.

text.p: Major crude oil producer Nigeria could come to a virtual standstill this week if a fuel shortage which has plagued the nation for more than a month does not ease, industry sources said on Sunday.
Few filling stations are still dispensing fuel for the six-million population of Lagos, commercial hub of a nation which pumps roughly two million barrels per day (bpd) of crude.
"More than three-quarters of the petrol stations in Lagos have no fuel," said pump attendant Mufu Rotibi.
Public transport has been crippled as lack of fuel has forced many operators to park their buses while fuel depots are besieged by road tankers which can't find fuel to load.
The road tanker drivers union on Saturday called on the government to take urgent steps to end the fuel scarcity.
State radio quoted a union spokesman as saying less than 200 trucks were being now loaded with fuel daily compared with 2,000 at normal times.
Rows and rows of immobile vehicles can be seen at pump stations and some of their owners said they had been there for several days.
Local newspapers said the situation was the same in most parts of the sprawling West african country, Africa's most populous with 104 million people.
There has so far been no reports of disturbances over the fuel situation but industry sources said the situation was getting desperate.
"The resilience of industry and commerce as well as the people is getting to snapping point," commented Gboyega Akintunde, an oil marketing executive in Lagos.
There is no sign that the military government has any formula for ending the scarcity , which newspapers have variously labelled "a national shame," and "the great energy crisis."

The independent Guardian said embattled oil minister Dan Etete had met officials of state oil company Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC) and the oil unions NUPENG and PENGASSAN to discuss measures to tackle the fuel crisis.
But measures so far announced were only to closely monitor the movement of fuel and supervise sales by soldiers .
Etete has meanwhile been locked in a slanging match with other senior administration officials over the fuel crisis.

The oil minister was irked when finance minister Anthony Ani said last weekend there was nothing to show for huge sums of money released between 1994 to 1996 for oil projects including repairs of refineries.
Lagos state military administrator Colonel Mohammed Marwa, a close aide of military ruler General Sani Abacha, put the knife into Etete when he openly blamed the oil ministry and NNPC for the crisis.
Etete in a statement forcely disputed Ani's remarks calling them "a deliberate falsehood" while he told reporters at Lagos airport on Friday that Marwa's statement was "childish."
One opposition newspaper said Abacha had called Etete to order and asked him to get about redressing the fuel situation rather than waging a press war with senior public officials.
Nigeria has four oil refineries but suffers recurrent fuel shortages, with the current one the worst so far.
The four refineries have a combined capacity of 445,000 barrels of crude oil daily but produce only a fraction of their capacity due to deteriorating facilities.
Last year, the government cut the allocation to the refineries by 50,000 bpd to 250,000 bpd and NNPC officials say this is one of the reasons for the fuel shortage.

Other contradictory explanations by officials for the fuel crisis have been bandied around, including ageing refineries, non-compliance with refinery maintenance schedules and non-disbursement of budgeted funds for the refineries by the federal authorities.
Some have called for imports but say this is unlikely because of a ban by Abacha on imports since September last year.
Lagos residents said Monday will be a difficult day for workers as they struggle to go to work after the weekend.
"I am not looking forward to tommorrow because of the fuel crisis," said bank clerk Anthony Okpene, adding "Many people will just stay at home."
